strengths: Well-motivated core insight: Loss vectors naturally separate clients from different clusters; Figure 1 effectively motivates why this is more robust than minimum-loss assignment (IFCA's approach)

Practical robustness advantage: Eliminates stringent IFCA initialization requirement (models must be within Δ/2 of optimal); Figure 2 convincingly demonstrates robustness to different initialization strategies

Rigorous theoretical analysis for linear regression: Theorem 4.1 (single-round cluster recovery), Theorem 4.2 (exponential convergence), and supporting separation lemmas (A.1-A.2) with detailed proofs

Comprehensive experimental validation: Diverse datasets (image and text), multiple task types (supervised/unsupervised), extensive heterogeneity settings (4 label skews, feature skew, concept shift), 11 baselines; achieves near-perfect ARI on images in 2-3 rounds
Broad applicability: Works in both supervised and unsupervised settings, unlike most competing methods requiring labeled data
Honest evaluation: Includes ablation studies acknowledging that bipartite matching contributes significantly; discusses theory-practice gap in Remark A.12
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: Theory analyzes linear regression with Gaussian features; experiments use non-convex neural networks. Theory requires ortho-normal or Δ-proximal initialization; experiments use random initialization and show robustness—contradicting assumptions. No convergence analysis for non-convex setting

Restrictive theoretical conditions: Condition dK⁴polylog(M)=o(nM) is opaque and difficult to verify. Requires Δ≈1 and unit-norm optimal models. Assumption A.15 (nₖmₖ(ρ/(ρ+1))²≫polylog(K)) hard to satisfy in practice. Remark A.12 admits analysis only works for square-root loss vectors, but regular losses used in practice

Limited algorithmic novelty: Clustering based on loss vectors is straightforward. Combines k-means, bipartite matching, and federated aggregation—standard techniques. Ablation (Table 12) shows matching critical (4.3% drop), suggesting this component rather than clustering is the key contribution

Mixed experimental results: Text datasets underperform—FedAvg achieves 99.0±0.1 on Amazon Review vs. CLoVE's 86.8±0.4 (12% gap) without adequate explanation. Many improvements over IFCA are marginal with large baselines variances. Some baseline results suspiciously poor (FeSEM: 73.2 on MNIST vs. Local-only 99.5)

Unsubstantiated privacy claims: Section 3 asserts loss vectors 'do not reveal anything about their data'—unjustified; loss vectors leak data distribution information. No formal privacy analysis or differential privacy guarantees provided, weakening practical applicability for sensitive applications

Experimental design concerns: Fixed learning rate γ=10⁻³ across all experiments—is this universally optimal or does it favor CLoVE? Small scale (20-100 clients, 4-10 clusters) vs. practical FL (thousands of clients). No statistical significance testing. Unclear if baselines received equal hyperparameter tuning

Insufficient failure mode analysis: Limited discussion of scenarios where CLoVE fails: when optimal models aren't well-separated, when clusters have heterogeneous internal distributions, or when K is misspecified. No guidance on method limitations

Missing complexity analysis: No communication cost or computational complexity comparison with baselines. Bipartite matching adds overhead not discussed. Small-scale experiments don't demonstrate scaling properties

Presentation gaps: Dense paper with critical details relegated to appendix. Theory-practice gap between linear regression (theory) and neural networks (experiments) not clearly bridged. Lemma A.17 (IFCA comparison) in appendix despite conceptual importance

strengths: Novel and intuitive approach using loss vectors for client clustering, avoiding IFCA's stringent initialization requirements
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets, task types, and heterogeneity scenarios with extensive baseline comparisons
Strong empirical results on clustering accuracy (near-perfect ARI in most cases) and image classification tasks
Formal theoretical analysis for linear regression with convergence guarantees (Theorems 4.1-4.2)
Demonstrates robustness to model initialization variations (Figure 2) compared to IFCA
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: Theory requires linear regression with specific assumptions (unit-norm models, Δ≈1, σ≪1, Eq. 7 condition never verified), while experiments use neural networks on real data where assumptions don't hold
Core assumption of loss vector separation is never formally verified on experimental datasets; only anecdotal justification in Figure 1
Problematic IFCA comparison: Tests IFCA with random initialization (against its design), making the comparison unfair; no fair comparison with proper initialization
Inconsistent empirical results contradicting main claims: FedAvg outperforms CLoVE on Amazon Reviews (99.0 vs 86.8), FlexCFL outperforms on AG News (60.2 vs 55.1)
Critical components lack theoretical justification: Bipartite matching (4.3% impact) and square root loss transformation (shown irrelevant in Table 12) lack principled explanations
No analysis of failure modes: Missing experiments on misspecified K, severely imbalanced clusters, or when loss vector separation assumption fails
Weak privacy claims: Statement that loss vectors reveal no data information is unproven; no formal privacy analysis despite being important for federated settings
Missing scalability analysis: Experiments use only 20-100 clients; behavior on thousands of clients (typical federated setting) unknown
Limited theoretical scope: Assumptions are highly restrictive (each client in cluster k uses exactly n_k samples, vague cluster balance condition); constants in bounds not characterized
Unjustified design choices: Explains square root loss is 'for analytical convenience' per Remark A.12, yet empirical ablations show no difference, suggesting overcomplication

strengths: Clear motivation and problem formulation: Figure 1 effectively demonstrates IFCA's failure mode and why loss-vector-based clustering provides a more robust solution
Elegant algorithmic simplicity: CLoVE is straightforward to implement and understand compared to gradient-based or prototype-based clustering alternatives

Robustness to initialization: Unlike IFCA's strict distance requirement (< Δ/2), CLoVE only requires ortho-normal or Δ-proximal models, with Figure 2 convincingly demonstrating consistency across initialization strategies

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple datasets (images and text), both supervised and unsupervised settings, diverse data heterogeneity scenarios (4 label skew types, feature skew, concept shift), and 10+ baseline comparisons
Unified framework for supervised and unsupervised learning: Applicability to both settings is rare and valuable in CFL literature
Consistent perfect/near-perfect clustering accuracy: ARI results show CLoVE achieves optimal clustering in nearly all experimental scenarios (Table 2)
Theoretical convergence analysis: Theorems 4.1-4.2 provide non-trivial guarantees including single-shot cluster recovery and exponential convergence for linear regression
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: All convergence guarantees (Theorems 4.1-4.2) apply exclusively to linear regression; neural network experiments lack theoretical backing. Condition dK⁴polylog(M) = o(nM) is restrictive and impractical for high-dimensional settings

Loss vector separation assumption unvalidated: Core assumption that clients in different clusters exhibit distinct loss patterns is intuitive but never formally validated empirically. No analysis of when/why separation might fail

Modest model accuracy improvements: While clustering accuracy excels, model accuracy gains over IFCA are often marginal or within error bars (e.g., Table 1: MNIST improvements 0.7%, CIFAR-10 2-5%). Amazon Reviews shows FedAvg outperforming CLoVE substantially (99.0 vs 86.8)

Insufficient privacy analysis: Brief dismissal in Section 3 claiming loss vectors reveal nothing about data ignores that loss patterns indirectly leak distributional information. Inadequate treatment for a federated learning paper

Initialization claims overclaimed: Despite framing as 'eliminating need for initialization,' the method still requires ortho-normal or Δ-proximal models as specific initialization requirements. Figure 2 shows convergence speed remains initialization-dependent
Unknown number of clusters K: Assumes K is known a priori, but this is unrealistic. No discussion, experiments, or sensitivity analysis for unknown K
Missing scalability analysis: Loss vectors have dimension K; scalability with large K (>10) unknown. Most experiments use K≤10. High-dimensional clustering may suffer but is unexplored

Text classification weakness unexplained: Surprisingly poor performance on Amazon Reviews (CLoVE 86.8 vs FedAvg 99.0) lacks investigation. AG News results also less impressive than image tasks, suggesting domain-specific limitations
Communication cost not analyzed: Each round requires K loss values per client, but communication cost comparison with baselines and convergence-in-rounds analysis are missing
Imbalanced cluster performance unknown: All experiments use balanced clusters. Performance with realistic imbalanced cluster distributions is unexplored

Ablation studies limited: Main ablation (Table 12) relegated to appendix. Square root loss variant theoretically required (Remark A.12) shows no practical benefit, suggesting theory-practice misalignment. Why bi-partite matching is critical deserves deeper investigation

Restrictive theoretical assumptions: Unit-norm optimal models, small noise (σ≪1), Δ close to 1, and Assumption A.15 requiring n_k m_k(ρ/(ρ+1))² ≫ polylog(K) may not hold in practice, especially with small clusters or high noise

strengths: Novel loss vector embedding approach: The insight that model losses separate clusters better than raw data is well-motivated and elegant, with clear intuition provided through examples.
Eliminates careful initialization requirement: Robustness to poor model initialization (Figure 2) is a significant practical advantage over IFCA, addressing a real limitation of prior work.
Solid theoretical contributions: Rigorous analysis for linear regression (Theorem 4.1-4.2) with formal convergence guarantees, building on established clustering theory.
Broad applicability and versatility: First method to handle both supervised and unsupervised CFL through autoencoders; works with any differentiable loss function.

Exceptionally comprehensive experimental evaluation: 6 datasets, 7 data heterogeneity scenarios, 10+ baselines, supervised and unsupervised settings, extensive ablations demonstrating consistent strong performance.
Rapid and reliable convergence: Achieves ARI ≥ 0.9 in 2-3 rounds consistently, substantially faster than most baselines (Table 3), with perfect clustering in most scenarios.
Practical efficiency: O(K) communication overhead per client for loss vectors; early stopping capability reduces long-term computational costs.
Clear presentation: Well-written with effective motivation, good intuition, and illustrative figures that convey key concepts clearly.
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: Theoretical guarantees limited to linear regression with Gaussian features; no analysis for neural networks with non-convex losses or complex data distributions used in experiments.

Restrictive theoretical assumptions: Requires minimum cluster separation Δ ≈ 1, very low noise (σ ≪ 1), high SNR (Δ²/σ² ≫ 1), and strong data volume conditions (nKm ≫ polylog terms). Unclear if these hold in practice.

Theorem 4.1 requires 'suitably initialized centers': Despite claims of not needing careful initialization, one-shot clustering still requires k-means centers initialized appropriately. Practical initialization procedure not specified.

Unknown cluster number (K) handling incomplete: selectBestK uses heuristic silhouette score without theoretical justification; occasional failures observed (Table 12: ARI=0.82); computational overhead of trying multiple K values not analyzed.

Privacy analysis underexplored: Paper acknowledges privacy implications 'remain underexplored'; loss vectors could enable distribution inference attacks; differential privacy deferred to future work; claims about non-sensitivity lack rigorous support.

Communication overhead analysis incomplete: While loss vectors are O(K), full communication complexity during clustering phase not provided; broadcasting K models to all M clients for multiple rounds could be substantial.

Experimental concerns: Some baselines show suspicious performance (FeSEM <15% on CIFAR-10, Table 1), raising fairness questions; limited to relatively small-scale datasets (mainly 20-50 clients, small K≤10); text classification shows competitive baselines.

Learning rate requires unknown parameter: Convergence proof requires η ≤ 1/2(1 - Δ/12) but Δ is unknown in practice; convergence rate constant c₁ unspecified; no guidance on practical hyperparameter selection.
Limited failure mode analysis: Few scenarios where CLoVE underperforms; insufficient discussion of when loss vector separation breaks down; unclear boundary conditions for algorithm success.
Stability detection informal: 3-round stability threshold lacks theoretical justification; clients declaring stability could lead to premature convergence in dynamic settings.

strengths: Clear motivation with effective intuition (Figure 1) explaining advantages over IFCA
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets, heterogeneity types, and both supervised/unsupervised settings
Demonstrates practical benefits: fast convergence (2-3 rounds), robustness to initialization, handling of stragglers
Provides formal theoretical analysis for linear regression case with convergence guarantees
Extensive ablation studies and robustness analyses in appendix showing consistency
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: convergence guarantees only for linear regression with restrictive assumptions (Δ≈1, SNR>>1, dK⁴polylog(M)=o(nM)); no theory for the general supervised/unsupervised settings tested

Core assumption insufficiently justified: why loss vectors should separate clusters better than raw data is only proven for linear regression; circular reasoning when using poorly-initialized models as clustering basis

Suspicious experimental comparisons: FeSEM achieves 11.2% on CIFAR-10 (implementation issue?), CFL-S shows 82.5±21.8% variance, text classification improvements are marginal (Amazon: 99.0% vs 99.0%, AG News: 84.1-86.8%)
Algorithm relies on heuristics: silhouette score for K-selection lacks justification, stability criterion 'set number of rounds' is unspecified, Khat selection in unknown K setting is ad-hoc

Communication/computational overhead inadequately analyzed: no concrete measurements of communication rounds or bytes during clustering phase; Appendix C.1 claims insignificance without supporting data
Privacy claims unsupported: Appendix C.2 admits analysis is 'underexplored'; no formal privacy analysis despite claiming privacy benefits
Limited unsupervised evaluation: only autoencoders on image datasets; no diverse unsupervised tasks beyond image reconstruction

strengths: Novel application of loss vector embeddings for client clustering with clear practical advantages over IFCA (no careful initialization needed) and CFL-S (convergence in 2-3 rounds vs. hundreds)
Applicable to both supervised and unsupervised settings, which is rare for CFL methods and demonstrated on autoencoders
Comprehensive experimental evaluation covering multiple datasets, extensive heterogeneity scenarios (label skew, feature skew, concept shift), up to 1000 clients, and ablation studies
Strong empirical results: consistently achieves near-perfect clustering (ARI ≈ 1.0) in 2-3 rounds with competitive or superior model accuracy across all tasks
Solid theoretical contributions for linear regression (Theorems 4.1-4.2) with detailed proofs connecting loss vector separation to proximity conditions
Robustness to initialization clearly demonstrated (Figure 2), addressing a major practical limitation of IFCA
Practical features including early stopping once clusters stabilize and simple, implementable algorithm
Extensive supplementary material with detailed experimental setup, code availability promised, and reproducible hyperparameters
weaknesses: Theory restricted to linear regression with strong assumptions (orthonormal initialization, unit-norm optimal models, Δ≈1, σ≪1); significant gap between theory and practice on complex tasks like CIFAR-10 CNNs
Core technical contribution relatively incremental—standard k-means clustering on loss vectors; clustering algorithm and initialization strategy not fully specified, limiting reproducibility
Communication overhead from broadcasting K models until stabilization not formally analyzed; claimed mitigation (weight-sharing layers) not empirically evaluated
When K unknown, Algorithm 2 requires clustering for multiple K values and computing silhouette scores, but computational cost and robustness of K selection not analyzed (only Table 12)

Limited failure mode analysis: no deep investigation of performance degradation when clusters have similar distributions or when K is misspecified; Figure 3(a) shows degrading performance with small Δ but lacks analysis

Privacy treatment superficial: Section C.2 acknowledges loss vectors' privacy implications are 'underexplored' while claiming they're 'not privacy-sensitive' (contradictory); no formal privacy guarantees
Some baseline methods perform surprisingly poorly (FeSEM: 11.2% on CIFAR-10; CFL-S: 82.5±21.8 on MNIST) raising concerns about proper tuning; high variance in some IFCA results (85.7±6.5) unexplained
Experimental design choices not justified: Why T=100 rounds? Why τ=1 local epoch? Stability criterion (3 consecutive rounds) seems arbitrary with no sensitivity analysis
Limited ablation studies: k-means vs FINCH comparison (Table 18) provided, but k-means initialization strategy, other clustering algorithms, and bipartite matching robustness not explored
Incomplete baseline comparisons: Recent work (Licciardi et al. 2025, Vardhan et al. 2024) dismissed without direct empirical comparison; unclear if all methods hyperparameter-tuned equally
